title: The Man in the Closet

beats.text: Imagine beating Wall Street for twenty-eight years from a desk in a closet.
New York, nineteen fifty-five. Walter Schloss skipped college but learned from Benjamin Graham.
No tips. No connections. Just manuals, and over a hundred cheap, dull stocks.
Stocks so boring they'd put a cocktail party to sleep.
Yet his investors earn about sixteen percent a year. The market? About eight.
So how do you beat Wall Street from a closet?
You see, get two hundred twenty-five million people flipping coins every morning.
After twenty days, about two hundred are still winning. Geniuses!
But in nineteen eighty-four, a famous talk noticed so many big winners shared one teacher. Graham.
Walter's method fit on a coin: worth a dollar? Buy it for forty cents.
The coin-flippers needed luck. Walter just needed a discount.

facts.claim: Schloss shared Tweedy, Browne's office in a tiny closet-sized office (Buffett: a sub-lease on a portion of a closet); used a desk in their office
Schloss never went to college and took Benjamin Graham's courses (NYSE Institute / NY Institute of Finance), later worked at Graham-Newman
Left Graham-Newman and started his own partnership in 1955 (with $100,000)
No connections, not fed ideas; looks up the numbers in the manuals and sends for annual reports (Adam Smith, Supermoney 1972); minimal contact with management; Value Line and reports
Owned well over 100 stocks at a time; ~1,000 securities over his career, mostly of a lackluster type
1956 to Q1 1984 (28 years): limited partners 16.1% a year compounded vs S&P 500 8.4% (partnership gross 21.3%)
Buffett's 1984 Columbia talk/essay: 225 million Americans flip coins, a dollar each; after 20 days about 215 winners with over $1 million each
Winners disproportionately came from one intellectual village with a common patriarch, Ben Graham (Graham-and-Doddsville)
Schloss's approach as described by Buffett: if a business is worth a dollar and I can buy it for 40 cents, something good may happen
Schloss died in 2012 aged 95; Graham died 1976 (no living people as characters)

caption:
Walter Schloss never went to college. From 1955 he ran his own fund, for decades from a closet-sized office, bought over a hundred cheap, dull stocks and read the manuals instead of chasing tips.
1956-1984: about 16% a year for his investors vs about 8% for the S&P 500. Luck? Buffett's famous 1984 coin-flip talk said no.
